## Odds and Stakes {#sec-mcgrath-odds}

I can be brief about McGrath's second point, because I agree with more of it than he might expect. He's right that for a proposition whose probability is about as high as an empirical proposition gets, like *the accepted year of the Battle of Hastings is 1066*, losing knowledge will take high stakes. His arithmetic is sound: if the odds needed for knowledge of such a proposition are very high, then keeping losses absolutely small while pushing the threshold past those odds requires gains so tiny that nothing turns on them, and the natural ways of restoring the pressure make the stakes high again.

Indeed, I originally drafted the red-blue game using Hastings, and changed it because the intuitions weren't strong enough. When the blue sentence says 1066 was the year of Hastings, it isn't clearly irrational to play Blue-True, and the argument needs that judgment to be clear. So on the case itself we don't disagree; that's why it isn't the case in the book.

But this points to a methodological issue with the second half of his discussion. The argument from the red-blue game was never a dominance argument. I did not argue: Red-True is at least as likely to win as Blue-True, so playing Blue-True is irrational. If that were the argument, it would generalise the way McGrath fears, and his reductio would land: any time the red sentence is logically weaker, or merely more probable, the blue knowledge would vanish, including knowledge that 2+2=4. The premise was the case-specific judgment that playing Blue-True is really irrational when the blue sentence is about Agincourt and the red one is 2+2=4. That judgment doesn't survive substitution. If the blue sentence is *2+2 is less than 100* and the red is *2+2=4*, I don't think either play is irrational, so the argument says nothing about what's known. The same goes for his logical-strength pairs. It may well be true that a rational agent can prefer to bet on the logically weaker proposition; but a permissible preference for Red-True doesn't make Blue-True irrational, and only the irrationality of Blue-True gets the argument going. So there is no pressure here towards scepticism about arithmetic, because there was never a general principle that higher probability on red strips knowledge from blue.

Two related points before moving on. First, even in the Hastings case, where knowledge would disappear only in situations everyone would call high stakes, I deny that there is a tight connection between stakes and knowledge. What grounds the change in knowledge is the change in the odds, not the change in the stakes. It may be, as McGrath in effect shows, that for propositions like this there is no realistic way to lengthen the odds without raising the stakes. But that makes high stakes a reliable accompaniment of knowledge loss in these cases, not its ground.

Second, keeping stakes out of the foundations was part of the point. @AndersonHawthorne2019a argue that the notion of high stakes, clear enough in two-option cases, resists being made precise once a choice has three or more options, and that it is not obvious it can be made precise in a way that lets stakes-based versions of pragmatic encroachment work. McGrath knows this challenge well, having replied to it [@FantlMcGrath2019]. My view doesn't need to answer it. The theory is stated in terms of odds and interests; 'stakes' appears only in informal glosses. If knowledge loss is correlated with high stakes in some rough sense, but the notion of stakes is too vague to bear theoretical weight, that is a problem only for views that put weight on it.
